paragraphs.heading: Cloth made at home
paragraphs.text: Before the 1760s, making cloth in Britain was a cottage industry, carried out by workers in their own homes and mostly using flax and wool. A typical weaving family owned one handloom, worked by the man with a boy's help, while the wife, girls and other women spun enough yarn to keep it busy. Goods travelled around the country by packhorse or by rivers and canals. During the Industrial Revolution, cloth-making came to centre on south Lancashire and on towns either side of the Pennines.

paragraphs.heading: Cotton from India
paragraphs.text: Cotton cloth was not new. India had a textile industry that made cotton goods, and in the second half of the 1600s the East India Company's factories in South Asia began sending finished cotton goods to Britain in quantity. These calicoes and chintzes competed with wool and linen. Local weavers, spinners, dyers, shepherds and farmers lobbied Parliament to ban their import, and later their sale.

paragraphs.heading: Spinning falls behind
paragraphs.text: John Kay's flying shuttle, from the 1730s, let a loom weave cloth faster and wider, doubling its output. Spinning could not keep up. Neither the simple spinning wheel nor the more refined Saxony wheel could make enough thread for the faster looms.

paragraphs.heading: Spinning moves into mills
paragraphs.text: Spinning was the first part of the trade to move into mills, and weaving followed later. A water-powered silk mill that John Lombe built at Derby in 1717 was arguably Britain's first successful highly mechanised factory. For cotton came the spinning jenny of James Hargreaves, the water frame of Richard Arkwright, and Samuel Crompton's spinning mule, which combined the two. These larger machines sat in water-powered mills on streams, and when a 1769 patent ran out in 1783, many cotton mills went up quickly.

paragraphs.heading: Steam frees the mills
paragraphs.text: James Watt's improved steam engine, patented in 1775, at first mostly pumped mines and water supplies, but from the 1780s it drove machines. That allowed efficient, semi-automated factories on a vast new scale in places where water power was missing or unsteady through the seasons. Mills and ironworks could now be built where other resources were handy, not just beside water. Early engines had poor speed control, which broke threads in spinning, but one fix was to have the engine pump water over a water wheel that drove the machines.

paragraphs.heading: Cotton takes the lead
paragraphs.text: Cotton overtook silk, wool and linen to become the most important textile. The hunger for power led to steam beam engines and mill engines that drove line shafts on every floor. Spare power encouraged more advanced power looms, set up in weaving sheds, the name for mills that specialised in weaving. Even so, by the 1820s, when all cotton, wool and worsted was spun in mills, the yarn still went out to weavers working at home. Around Manchester, output grew so large that the mill towns needed a cotton exchange and warehouses.
